desc:
Buildings stand in a row from west to east; heights[i] is the height of building i, and the sun sets in the east, to the right of the last building. A building has a sunset view if it is strictly taller than every building to its right (the last building always has one).

Return the indices of all buildings with a sunset view, in increasing order.

Example: heights = [4, 2, 3, 1] gives [0, 2, 3]: building 1 (height 2) is blocked by the taller building 2.
constraints: A building of equal height to one on its right is blocked
hints: Building i is blocked exactly when some building to its right is at least as tall.
Think about it from the other direction: sweep from the sun side and remember the tallest height seen so far. Or sweep left to right and let a taller building knock out the buildings it blocks.
Left to right with a stack of indices: while the top building is not taller than the new one, pop it (it is blocked); then push the new index. The stack at the end is the answer.
editorial: Use a monotonic stack of indices whose heights are strictly decreasing from bottom to top. When building i arrives, every building on the stack with height ≤ heights[i] now has a building at least as tall to its right, so it can never have a sunset view; pop it. Afterwards push i.

A building that is never popped has no building at least as tall to its right, which is exactly the sunset-view condition. So the final stack, read bottom to top, is the answer already in increasing index order. Time is O(n) and space O(n). A right-to-left sweep that tracks the running maximum gives the same result in O(1) extra space, but the stack version shows the general pattern.
